Homarus gammarus , known as the European lobster or common lobster , is a species of clawed lobster from the eastern Atlantic Ocean , Mediterranean Sea and parts of the Black Sea . It is closely related to the American lobster , H. americanus . It may grow to a length of 60 cm ( 24 in ) and a mass of 6 kilograms ( 13 lb ) , and bears a conspicuous pair of claws . In life , the lobsters are blue , only becoming " lobster red " on cooking . Mating occurs in the summer , producing eggs which are carried by the females for up to a year before hatching into planktonic larvae . Homarus gammarus is a highly esteemed food , and is widely caught using lobster pots , mostly around the British Isles . 
 Homarus gammarus is a large crustacean , with a body length up to 60 centimetres ( 24 in ) and weighing up to 5 – 6 kilograms ( 11 – 13 lb ) , although the lobsters caught in lobster pots are usually 23 – 38 cm ( 9 – 15 in ) long and weigh 0 @.@ 7 – 2 @.@ 2 kg ( 1 @.@ 5 – 4 @.@ 9 lb ) . Like other crustaceans , lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed in order to grow , in a process called ecdysis ( moulting ) . This may occur several times a year for young lobsters , but decreases to once every 1 – 2 years for larger animals . 
 The first pair of pereiopods is armed with a large , asymmetrical pair of claws . The larger one is the " crusher " , and has rounded nodules used for crushing prey ; the other is the " cutter " , which has sharp inner edges , and is used for holding or tearing the prey . Usually , the left claw is the crusher , and the right is the cutter . 
 The exoskeleton is generally blue above , with spots that coalesce , and yellow below . The red colour associated with lobsters only appears after cooking . This occurs because , in life , the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex , but the complex is broken up by the heat of cooking , releasing the red pigment . 
 The closest relative of H. gammarus is the American lobster , Homarus americanus . The two species are very similar , and can be crossed artificially , although hybrids are unlikely to occur in the wild since their ranges do not overlap .  Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimetres ( 3 @.@ 1 – 3 @.@ 3 in ) , whereas males mature at a slightly smaller size . Mating typically occurs in summer between a recently moulted female , whose shell is therefore soft , and a hard @-@ shelled male . The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months , depending on the temperature , attached to her pleopods . Females carrying eggs are said to be " berried " and can be found throughout the year . 
 The eggs hatch at night , and the larvae swim to the water surface where they drift with the ocean currents , preying on zooplankton . This stage involves three moults and lasts for 15 – 35 days . After the third moult , the juvenile takes on a form closer to the adult , and adopts a benthic lifestyle . The juveniles are rarely seen in the wild , and are poorly known , although they are known to be capable of digging extensive burrows . It is estimated that only 1 larva in every 20 @,@ 000 survives to the benthic phase . When they reach a carapace length of 15 mm ( 0 @.@ 59 in ) , the juveniles leave their burrows and start their adult lives .

It is also present in most of the Mediterranean Sea , only missing from the section east of Crete , and along only the north @-@ west coast of the Black Sea .  The species can be divided into four genetically distinct populations , one widespread population , and three which have diverged due to small effective population sizes , possibly due to adaptation to the local environment . The first of these is the population of lobsters from northern Norway , which have been referred to as the " midnight @-@ sun lobster " . The populations in the Mediterranean Sea are distinct from those in the Atlantic Ocean . The last distinct population is found in the Netherlands : samples from the <unk> were distinct from those collected in the North Sea or English Channel . 
 Attempts have been made to introduce H. gammarus to New Zealand , alongside other European species such as the edible crab , Cancer pagurus . Between 1904 and 1914 , one million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin , but the species did not become established there . 
 Adult H. gammarus live on the continental shelf at depths of 0 – 150 metres ( 0 – 492 ft ) , although not normally deeper than 50 m ( 160 ft ) . They prefer hard substrates , such as rocks or hard mud , and live in holes or crevices , emerging at night to feed .

 Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam , CB , CBE ( 15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976 ) was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force ( RAAF ) . Born and educated in Tasmania , he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 . He specialised in flying instruction and navigation before the outbreak of World War II . In April 1941 , he became commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron , which operated Lockheed Hudsons . The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December , and saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific . After returning to Australia in February 1942 , Headlam held staff appointments and training commands , finishing the war a group captain . 
 Headlam served as Officer Commanding North @-@ Western Area in 1946 , and as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950 . In 1950 – 51 , during the Malayan Emergency , he was stationed at Singapore as commander of No. 90 ( Composite ) Wing and , later , RAF Tengah . He twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel , in 1957 and 1959 – 60 , receiving appointment as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958 . Promoted air vice marshal , he successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) Operational Command in 1961 – 62 , AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia – Malaysia Konfrontasi , Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965 – 66 , and AOC Support Command in 1966 – 67 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965 . Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971 , he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later . 
 The son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam , Frank Headlam was born on 15 July 1914 in Launceston , Tasmania . He was schooled at <unk> College , Hobart , and matriculated in 1932 . He underwent flying instruction with No. 1 Flying Training School ( FTS ) at RAAF Point Cook , Victoria , and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935 .

No larger than a flight according to the official history of the pre @-@ war RAAF , Seaplane Squadron was part of No. 1 FTS and operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes , among other types . During this posting Headlam was promoted to flying officer , on 1 July 1935 , and wrote a paper on national defence in which he suggested that with " strong air forces , naval forces ( including submarines ) , and fixed defences , Australia may be made practically invulnerable " . According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens , this paper " in effect , defined the ' anti @-@ lodgment ' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking " . 
 Headlam completed a flying instructors course in July 1936 and joined the staff of No. 1 FTS . He was promoted to flight lieutenant on 1 March 1937 . Commencing in July 1938 , he was one of six students to take part in the RAAF 's first Long Specialist Navigation Course , run by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook . The course involved several epic training flights that attracted considerable media attention , including a twelve @-@ day , 10 @,@ 800 @-@ kilometre ( 6 @,@ 700 mi ) round @-@ Australia trip by three Avro Ansons , one of which was piloted by Headlam , in November . The following month , Headlam led the three Ansons on a six @-@ day journey back and forth over Central Australia . He subsequently passed the navigation course with a special distinction . On 27 January 1939 he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton , Victoria , as a flight commander . He served initially with No. 2 Squadron , before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on 29 August . Both units operated Ansons . 
 Following the outbreak of World War II , No. 1 Squadron was engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance duties off south @-@ eastern Australia . Headlam continued to serve with the squadron as a flight commander until 15 January 1940 , when he was assigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer . On 27 March he was posted to the staff of RAAF Headquarters , Melbourne . He was promoted to squadron leader on 1 June 1940 . Two weeks later he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul 's Anglican Church in Frankston ; the couple would have a son and a daughter . 
 Headlam was given command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 , and raised to wing commander on 1 July . Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons , the squadron mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December , when four of its aircraft were ordered to Darwin , Northern Territory , in response to fears of Japanese aggression in the Pacific . On 7 December , this detachment established itself at Penfui , near Koepang in Dutch Timor , while No. 2 Squadron 's eight remaining Hudsons were stationed at Darwin on standby . The following day , aware that Australia was now at war in the Pacific , one of the Penfui @-@ based Hudsons attacked the Japanese <unk> Nanyo Maru , which was suspected of being a radio ship , and forced it aground . By 12 December , Headlam had transferred to Penfui as commanding officer of the base , as well as No. 2 Squadron .

Eastern Area Command , considered a de facto operational headquarters owing to the preponderance of combat units under its control , was reorganised as Home Command in October 1953 . He was promoted to acting air commodore in May . His appointment as aide @-@ de @-@ camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on 7 October 1954 . 
 Headlam was promoted to substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955 . In November he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters , London , and the following year undertook studies at the Imperial Defence College . Returning to Australia , he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air , Canberra , from 19 March to 21 October 1957 , between the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters , and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960 , between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely . In this role Headlam occupied a seat on the Air Board , the service 's controlling body that comprised its senior officers and was chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff . He was also one of two RAAF representatives to serve on a committee , chaired by businessman William John Allison , examining conditions of defence service ; the committee 's recommendations led to a doubling of flight pay , among other improvements . Headlam 's other positions at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959 , and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959 . The latter assignment put him in charge of the RAAF 's Directorate of Intelligence . Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire ( CBE ) in the 1958 Queen 's Birthday Honours , gazetted on 3 June . In May 1960 he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff . 
 On 30 January 1961 , Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command ( OPCOM ) , the successor organisation to Home Command , responsible for the direction of RAAF operational units . He took over as Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April . Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on 29 May . On 17 July 1962 , he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth , Malaya , and took up the appointment of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore one week later . He was succeeded as AOC OPCOM by Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch . As AOC No. 224 Group , Headlam had overall responsibility for regional air defence and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 , and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the following month . Divorced from his first wife in 1956 , he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on 20 January 1964 . He handed over No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on 30 November . 
 Returning to Australia , Headlam became Deputy Chief of the Air Staff ( DCAS ) on 26 January 1965 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath ( CB ) " in recognition of distinguished service in the Borneo Territories " on 22 June . His tenure as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament program the Air Force had undertaken since World War II , and with manpower shortages stemming from this expansion and from Australia 's increasing involvement in the security of South East Asia . The first RAAF helicopters were committed to the Vietnam War towards the end of his term , and he travelled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff , Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton , in March 1966 to plan the deployment . The year before , Wilton had recommended to Air Marshal Murdoch , the Chief of the Air Staff , that two Iroquois be sent to Vietnam for familiarisation purposes ; Murdoch had rebuffed Wilton , and the RAAF helicopter squadron was considered underprepared for its army co @-@ operation role when it finally did deploy . On 1 January 1968 , Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff . He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971 . 
 Returning to Australia in June 1971 , Headlam took resettlement leave before retiring from the Air Force on 3 August . He made his home in Melbourne , where he died aged 62 on 23 December 1976 , after a lengthy battle with cancer . Survived by his children and his second wife , he was given a private funeral and cremated at Springvale Crematorium .

 The current M @-@ 82 dates back to 1926 . It ran from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City . rewritten: The European lobster, scientifically named *Homarus gammarus*, is a clawed lobster species inhabiting the eastern Atlantic Ocean, the Mediterranean Sea, and portions of the Black Sea. This species shares a close relationship with the American lobster, *H. americanus*. European lobsters can reach lengths of up to 60 cm (24 in) and weigh as much as 6 kilograms (13 lb), characterized by their prominent claws. While alive, they exhibit a blue coloration, transforming into the familiar "lobster red" only after being cooked. Mating takes place during the summer months, resulting in eggs that females carry for almost a year before they hatch into planktonic larvae. *Homarus gammarus* is considered a delicacy and is commonly captured using lobster pots, particularly in the waters surrounding the British Isles.

The European lobster, *Homarus gammarus*, is a sizable crustacean that can reach a body length of 60 cm (24 in) and a weight of 5–6 kg (11–13 lb). However, lobsters typically caught in traps measure 23–38 cm (9–15 in) in length and weigh between 0.7–2.2 kg (1.5–4.9 lb). Similar to other crustaceans, lobsters possess a rigid exoskeleton that they must shed to facilitate growth, a process known as ecdysis or moulting. Younger lobsters may moult several times annually, while larger individuals moult less frequently, typically once every 1–2 years.

The first set of pereiopods features sizable, dissimilar claws. The larger claw, known as the "crusher," possesses rounded bumps for pulverizing prey, while the other, the "cutter," has keen inner edges used to secure or rip apart food. Typically, the left claw functions as the crusher, and the right claw serves as the cutter.

Lobsters typically exhibit a blue coloration on their upper exoskeleton with merging spots, and a yellow underside. The familiar red hue only emerges upon cooking. This transformation happens because the red pigment, astaxanthin, is naturally masked by a protein complex. The heat from cooking breaks down this complex, liberating the red pigment and revealing the lobster's characteristic cooked color.

The European lobster, H. gammarus, shares a close kinship with the American lobster, Homarus americanus. These two species exhibit remarkable similarities and are capable of interbreeding under artificial conditions. However, natural hybridization is improbable due to their geographically separated habitats. Distinguishing between the two species relies on several key characteristics.

Female European lobsters (Homarus gammarus) become sexually mature at a carapace length of 80–85 mm (3.1–3.3 in), while males mature at a slightly smaller size. Mating usually takes place in the summer months, involving a recently molted, soft-shelled female and a hard-shelled male. The female carries the eggs, attached to her pleopods, for as long as 12 months, depending on the water temperature. Females carrying eggs are known as "berried" and can be observed year-round.

At night, the eggs hatch, releasing larvae that ascend to the water's surface. These larvae then drift with ocean currents, feeding on zooplankton. This larval phase involves three molting stages and lasts between 15 and 35 days. Following the third molt, the juvenile form more closely resembles the adult and transitions to a benthic existence. These juveniles are infrequently observed in their natural habitat and remain largely unstudied, though they are known to create complex burrow systems. It is estimated that only a tiny fraction of larvae, about 1 in 20,000, survive to reach the benthic stage. Once the juveniles attain a carapace length of 15 mm (0.59 in), they emerge from their burrows and begin their adult lives.

The European lobster, Homarus gammarus, inhabits the northeastern Atlantic Ocean, ranging from northern Norway to the Azores and Morocco, but is absent from the Baltic Sea. Its distribution includes the majority of the Mediterranean Sea, except for the area east of Crete, and extends only along the northwestern coast of the Black Sea. The species' northernmost limits are within the Norwegian fjords, inside the Arctic Circle.

This species comprises four genetically different groups: a common, widespread population and three others that have evolved separately, likely due to limited population sizes and adaptation to specific local conditions. One of these unique groups is the lobster population in northern Norway, sometimes called the "midnight sun lobster." Lobsters in the Mediterranean Sea also form a distinct population compared to those in the Atlantic Ocean. The final distinct group is located in the Netherlands, where samples from the <unk> differed genetically from those taken in the North Sea or English Channel.

Efforts were undertaken to establish the European lobster, H. gammarus, in New Zealand, concurrent with the introduction of other European species like the edible crab, Cancer pagurus. During the period spanning 1904 to 1914, a million lobster larvae originating from hatcheries in Dunedin were released; however, the species failed to establish a population.

European lobsters (H. gammarus) inhabit the continental shelf at depths ranging from 0 to 150 meters (0 to 492 ft), but are most commonly found at depths less than 50 m (160 ft). These lobsters favor firm surfaces like rocks or compacted mud, where they take shelter in natural openings and cracks, venturing out to forage for food during the night.

The European lobster, Homarus gammarus, is vulnerable to gaffkaemia, a disease caused by the bacterium Aerococcus viridans. While commonly observed in American lobsters, this disease has only been reported in captive H. gammarus, and in these instances, the possibility of prior occupancy of the tanks by American lobsters (H. americanus) could not be excluded.

*Homarus gammarus* has long been considered a culinary delicacy, even appearing in a 17th-century English folk song. It can command premium prices and is available fresh, frozen, canned, or powdered. Its claws and abdomen offer high-quality white meat, and the majority of the cephalothorax is also edible, with the exception of the gastric mill and digestive tract. *H. gammarus* can cost significantly more than *H. americanus*, with many believing the European lobster possesses a superior taste.

Lobsters are primarily caught using lobster pots, but they can also be lured out with octopus or cuttlefish-baited lines, enabling capture with a net or by hand. In 2008, European and North African fisheries yielded 4,386 tonnes of *H. gammarus*, with the British Isles (including the Channel Islands) accounting for 3,462 tonnes (79%) of the total. The legal minimum size for landing *H. gammarus* is a carapace length of 87 mm (3.4 in).

*Homarus gammarus* is the designated type species for the genus *Homarus* Weber, 1795, a decision made by Direction 51 of the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature. Before this designation, the species was known by various names, such as *Astacus marinus* Fabricius, 1775, and *Homarus vulgaris* H. Milne-Edwards, 1837, causing confusion. This was further complicated by the fact that Friedrich Weber's original genus description was not recognized until Mary Rathbun rediscovered it, invalidating any previous type species designations (for *Homarus* H. Milne-Edwards, 1837) for *Homarus* Weber, 1795.

In 1974, Holthuis designated a lectotype as the type specimen for Homarus gammarus. This specimen originated from waters near Marstrand, Sweden (57°53′ N 11°32′ E), approximately 48 kilometers (30 miles) northwest of Gothenburg. Regrettably, both the lectotype and the  have been lost since then.

Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam, CB, CBE (15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976), was a high-ranking officer in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF). He was born and received his early education in Tasmania before enlisting in the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934. Prior to World War II, he focused on developing expertise in both flight instruction and navigation. In April 1941, he took command of No. 2 Squadron, equipped with Lockheed Hudsons. The squadron was sent to Dutch Timor in December and participated in operations against Japanese troops in the South West Pacific. Headlam returned to Australia in February 1942 and served in various staff and training roles, ultimately reaching the rank of group captain by the end of the war.

In 1946, Headlam commanded the North-Western Area, followed by a term as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950. During the Malayan Emergency in 1950–51, he was based in Singapore, commanding No. 90 (Composite) Wing and subsequently RAF Tengah. He twice filled the role of acting Air Member for Personnel, once in 1957 and again from 1959 to 1960, and was made a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958. He was promoted to air vice marshal and successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding (AOC) Operational Command (1961–62), AOC No. 224 Group RAF (1962–1965) during the Indonesia–Malaysia Konfrontasi, Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (1965–66), and AOC Support Command (1966–67). In 1965, he was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath. After serving as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff in London from 1968 to 1971, he retired from the Air Force and passed away in Melbourne five years later.

Frank Headlam, born in Launceston, Tasmania, on July 15, 1914, was the son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam. He received his education at <unk> College in Hobart, completing his matriculation in 1932. Defying his parents' desires, he enlisted in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) as an air cadet on January 16, 1934. He received flight training at No. 1 Flying Training School (FTS) located at RAAF Point Cook, Victoria, and was subsequently commissioned as a pilot officer on January 1, 1935.

Following his conversion course, Headlam was posted to the Seaplane Squadron at Point Cook. This squadron, considered a flight in size by the official pre-war RAAF history, was a component of No. 1 FTS and utilized aircraft such as Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes. While stationed here, Headlam was promoted to flying officer on July 1, 1935, and authored a paper on national defense. In it, he proposed that Australia could achieve near invulnerability through "strong air forces, naval forces (including submarines), and fixed defenses." Air Force historian Alan Stephens asserts that this paper "in effect, defined the 'anti-lodgment' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking."

After finishing a flying instructors course in July 1936, Headlam became a staff member at No. 1 FTS. He was then promoted to flight lieutenant on March 1, 1937. Starting in July 1938, Headlam was among six students selected for the RAAF's inaugural Long Specialist Navigation Course, instructed by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook. This course featured remarkable training flights that garnered significant media coverage, including a 12-day, 10,800-kilometer (6,700 mi) journey around Australia in November by three Avro Ansons, with Headlam piloting one of them. The next month, Headlam led the three Ansons on a six-day round trip over Central Australia. He later completed the navigation course with special recognition. On January 27, 1939, he was assigned to RAAF Station Laverton, Victoria, as a flight commander, initially serving with No. 2 Squadron before moving to No. 1 Squadron on August 29. Both squadrons were equipped with Ansons.

After World War II began, No. 1 Squadron performed convoy escort and maritime surveillance tasks off the southeastern coast of Australia. Headlam remained with the squadron as a flight commander until January 15, 1940, at which point he was transferred to Headquarters Laverton to work as the station navigation officer. On March 27, he was reassigned to the staff at RAAF Headquarters in Melbourne. He received a promotion to squadron leader on June 1, 1940. He married Katherine Bridge at St Paul's Anglican Church in Frankston two weeks later, and they went on to have a son and a daughter.

On April 15, 1941, Headlam assumed command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton and was promoted to wing commander on July 1. The squadron, equipped with Lockheed Hudsons, primarily carried out maritime patrols in southern waters until December 5. Due to growing concerns about Japanese aggression in the Pacific, four of its planes were dispatched to Darwin, Northern Territory. On December 7, this detachment set up operations at Penfui, near Koepang in Dutch Timor, while the remaining eight Hudsons of No. 2 Squadron were kept on standby in Darwin. The next day, with Australia now at war in the Pacific, a Hudson based at Penfui attacked the Japanese Nanyo Maru, suspected of being a radio ship, and ran it aground. By December 12, Headlam had moved to Penfui to serve as commanding officer of both the base and No. 2 Squadron.

In January 1942, No. 2 Squadron's planes were stationed across Penfui on <unk> Island, and Darwin. The Penfui group engaged Japanese ships involved in the Celebes invasion. On January 11, two Hudsons bombing a transport ship shot down or damaged three attacking Japanese floatplanes; however, on January 12, both Hudsons were downed by Mitsubishi Zeros. Penfui was first bombed by the Japanese on January 26, 1942, and suffered regular attacks, causing damage to some aircraft. The undamaged Hudsons were moved to Darwin, but Headlam and his team stayed at Penfui to support reconnaissance flights from Australia. On February 18, Headlam was instructed to evacuate all personnel except a small team to destroy the airfield with Sparrow Force's help. He returned to Darwin the next day, coinciding with the city's first Japanese air raid. Four of No. 2 Squadron's Hudsons were destroyed in the raid; the surviving planes were moved to Daly Waters, from where they continued reconnaissance and bombing missions against Japanese targets in Timor.

Headlam continued his service in Darwin as Controller of Operations at Headquarters North-Western Area Command until May 12, 1942, after which he was transferred to Nhill, Victoria, to take command of No. 2 Air Navigation School, which utilized Ansons. In June, No. 97 (Reserve) Squadron was created from the school's staff. On July 20, 1943, Headlam assumed command of No. 2 Air Observer School, also equipped with Ansons, in Mount Gambier, South Australia. He achieved the rank of group captain on December 1, 1943, and on December 9, he was made the first commanding officer of No. 3, operating Ansons and Fairey Battles from Port Pirie. Following his departure from No. 3, he began studies at the RAAF Staff School in Mount Martha, Victoria, on October 2, 1944. He was then appointed senior administrative staff officer at North-Western Area Command on January 12, 1945.

In January 1946, Headlam assumed command of the North-Western Area. After being stationed to Britain at the close of the year, he attended the Royal Air Force Staff College in Andover and was assigned to the RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London. Upon his return to Australia in November 1947, he was made Director of Training at RAAF Headquarters. Headlam's appointment to command No. 90 (Composite) Wing, succeeding Group Captain Paddy Heffernan, occurred in November 1950. Based at RAF Changi in Singapore, No. 90 Wing oversaw RAAF units involved in the Malayan Emergency: No. 1 (Bomber) Squadron, equipped with Avro Lincolns, and No. 38 (Transport) Squadron, operating Douglas C-47 Dakotas. The Lincolns carried out both area bombing operations over communist-controlled areas and precision strikes. The Dakotas performed various duties across Southeast Asia and within Malaya, including courier services, VIP transportation, medical evacuations, troop and cargo airlift, supply drops to allied forces, and the distribution of propaganda leaflets. On December 20, Headlam sustained minor injuries when a No. 38 Squadron Dakota he was co-piloting crash-landed at Kampong Aur in Pahang due to engine failure during a supply drop. In August 1951, he was appointed commander of RAF Tengah, Singapore, while retaining his position as commanding officer of No. 90 Wing. Headlam relinquished command of No. 90 Wing in December 1951.

In February 1952, Headlam assumed the role of senior air staff officer (SASO) at Eastern Area Command in Penrith, New South Wales. His time as SASO coincided with the RAAF's introduction of English Electric Canberra jet bombers and CAC Sabre jet fighters. A significant organisational restructuring also occurred, shifting the Air Force from a geographically-focused command structure to a functional one, leading to the creation of Home (operational), Training, and Maintenance Commands. Eastern Area Command, effectively an operational headquarters due to its large number of combat units, was subsequently reconfigured as Home Command in October 1953. Headlam's "exceptional ability and devotion to duty" were recognised in the 1954 New Year Honours with his appointment as an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE). He was promoted to acting air commodore in May, and his appointment as aide-de-camp to Queen Elizabeth II was made public on October 7, 1954.

Headlam achieved the rank of substantive air commodore on January 1, 1955. The following November, he was assigned to RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London, and in 1956, he attended the Imperial Defence College. Upon his return to Australia, he held the position of acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air in Canberra from March 19 to October 21, 1957, succeeding Air Vice Marshal Fred Scherger and preceding Allan Walters, and again from August 24, 1959, to March 28, 1960, succeeding Walters and preceding Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely. As Air Member for Personnel, Headlam was a member of the Air Board, the RAAF's governing body composed of senior officers and led by the Chief of the Air Staff. He also served as one of two RAAF representatives on a committee, led by William John Allison, that reviewed the conditions of service in the defence force; its recommendations resulted in a doubling of flight pay and other enhancements. At the Department of Air, Headlam also served as Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959, and as Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959. In the latter role, he oversaw the RAAF's Directorate of Intelligence. Headlam was made a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the Queen's Birthday Honours of 1958, which were announced on June 3. In May 1960, he was appointed acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff.

In January 1961, Headlam became part of Operational Command (OPCOM), the new organization replacing Home Command, which controlled RAAF operational units. He replaced Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock as Air Officer Commanding (AOC) OPCOM in April and was promoted to air vice marshal on May 29. On July 17, 1962, Headlam was assigned to RAAF Base Butterworth in Malaya, assuming the role of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore a week later. Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch took over from him as AOC OPCOM. As AOC No. 224 Group, Headlam oversaw regional air defense and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962, and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia, which officially started the following month. After divorcing his first wife in 1956, he married Vernon Spence, a widowed social worker, in Sydney on January 20, 1964. He relinquished command of No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on November 30.

Upon his return to Australia, Headlam assumed the role of Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (DCAS) on January 26, 1965. In recognition of his "distinguished service in the Borneo Territories," he was made a Companion of the Order of the Bath (CB) on June 22. His time as DCAS corresponded with the Air Force's most substantial rearmament effort since World War II, as well as personnel deficits caused by this expansion and Australia's growing participation in Southeast Asian security. Near the conclusion of his term, the initial RAAF helicopters were deployed to the Vietnam War, and in March 1966, he visited Saigon alongside Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton, the Chief of the General Staff, to coordinate the deployment. The previous year, Wilton had suggested to Air Marshal Murdoch, the Chief of the Air Staff, that two Iroquois helicopters be sent to Vietnam for familiarization; however, Murdoch rejected Wilton's proposal, resulting in the RAAF helicopter squadron being deemed inadequately prepared for its army cooperation mission upon deployment. On August 8, 1966, Headlam took over from Air Vice Marshal Douglas Candy as AOC Support Command in Melbourne. Support Command, which was established in 1959, was formed by combining the RAAF's former Training and Maintenance Commands. Headlam was assigned to London on January 1, 1968, as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff. From November 17, 1970, to June 5, 1971, he served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen.

Headlam came back to Australia in June 1971 and used resettlement leave before officially leaving the Air Force on August 3rd. He settled in Melbourne, where he passed away at the age of 62 on December 23, 1976, following a prolonged fight with cancer. He was survived by his children and his second wife, and his funeral was held privately, followed by cremation at Springvale Crematorium.

M-82 is a state highway located in Michigan's Lower Peninsula, connecting Fremont and Howard City. The segment between Newaygo and Howard City passes through Fremont and skirts the southern boundary of the Manistee National Forest. The existing M-82 is the second iteration of a highway with that designation in Michigan; the first M-82 was in the Upper Peninsula around 1919. The current Lower Peninsula route dates back to the 1920s. Throughout its history, M-82 has been extended and shortened, with its western terminus previously reaching New Era or Hesperia. The present-day alignment of the route was established in the late 1970s.

M-82 starts at a three-way intersection west of Fremont where M-120 and B-96 meet. This point also marks where three counties converge: Newaygo, Oceana, and Muskegon. M-120 runs north-south, delineating the Newaygo-Oceana and Newaygo-Muskegon county borders. B-96, forming the Oceana-Muskegon county line, extends westward from this intersection. From here, M-82 heads east along 48th Street, traversing farmland into Fremont. As it enters the town, the route becomes Main Street, proceeding through the central business district before turning south onto Stewart Avenue. Leaving Fremont, M-82 curves onto 72nd Street, continuing eastward through agricultural areas. Approaching Newaygo, the landscape becomes increasingly wooded near the Muskegon River. M-82 then follows Fremont Street east until it merges with M-37. The two routes run together across the river and into Newaygo's downtown along State Street. South of the city center, M-82 diverges east from M-37, becoming 82nd Street and running along the southern boundary of the Manistee National Forest. Its eastern terminus is at exit 118 on US 131/M-46, located west of Howard City.

As part of its routine maintenance, the Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT) monitors traffic volume on its roads, using a metric known as average annual daily traffic (AADT). AADT represents the average daily traffic volume on a specific road segment over a year. MDOT's 2009 data revealed that the highest traffic volume on M-82 was west of Fremont, with 16,532 vehicles per day. The lowest traffic volume was recorded east of Newaygo, with 4,018 vehicles daily. Furthermore, no portion of M-82 has been included in the National Highway System, a network of roads crucial for the nation's economy, defense, and transportation.

The M-82 highway, established in 1926, originally stretched from US 31 in Hart to the intersection of US 131 and M-46 in Howard City. Its path passed through Ferry, Hesperia, and Fremont, effectively taking over the former M-41 route. In late 1936, M-46 was extended along the Newaygo to Howard City segment, creating a shared M-46/M-82 route to complete a missing section of M-46. This overlap was eliminated in 1938, with M-82 truncated to its northern junction with M-37 in Newaygo, and the concurrent portion becoming solely M-46. In late 1947 or early 1948, M-82 was realigned west of Ferry, and instead of its original northwesterly course to Hart, it was directed westward to terminate in Shelby.

The highway's western end underwent two realignments in 1963 and 1964, redirecting it from Hesperia to New Era and bypassing Ferry. Around 1969, a more significant change occurred in Oceana County, altering highway designations. M-20 replaced M-82 west of Hesperia, terminating in New Era instead of Muskegon, while the new M-120 replaced M-20 south of Hesperia. Consequently, M-82's route was shortened to run solely from Hesperia to Newaygo. In 1973, the highway was extended eastward back to Howard City. M-46 was rerouted via the US 131 freeway south of Howard City to Cedar Springs, taking over the former M-57 between Cedar Springs and Casnovia. This change allowed the Newaygo to Howard City segment to revert to the M-82 designation. The final alteration happened in 1978 when the concurrency with M-120 was removed in favor of M-120, truncating M-82 to the junction west of Fremont, establishing the current highway route.

Shikamaru Nara is a character created by Masashi Kishimoto for the Naruto manga and anime series. Within the story, Shikamaru is a ninja from Konohagakure and a member of Team 10, which also includes Choji Akimichi, Ino Yamanaka, and their leader Asuma Sarutobi. He is depicted as a lazy individual who avoids using his remarkable intellect, a trait that Kishimoto has said he appreciates in Shikamaru. Beyond the main Naruto series, Shikamaru has been featured in four of the franchise's films, various video games, and original video animations related to the Naruto universe.

Shikamaru's character has been a popular subject of discussion in various anime and manga publications. Critics frequently mention his intelligence and indolence, as well as his development into a leadership role. Anime News Network lauded Shikamaru's evolution into "an unlikely hero" within the Naruto narrative. Shikamaru's popularity extends to Naruto fans, as evidenced by his consistently high rankings in popularity surveys. A range of Shikamaru-themed merchandise has been launched, including keychains, patches, and action figures.

Masashi Kishimoto has expressed his fondness for Shikamaru, appreciating his relaxed demeanor despite his genius-level intellect, a trait he contrasted with Sasuke Uchiha's intelligence coupled with his sharp personality. Kishimoto jokingly stated that, were he female, he would marry Shikamaru, predicting his future success. In designing Shikamaru's look for Part II, Kishimoto aimed for a distinctive appearance, even while using a vest common among ninja. To achieve this, he placed Shikamaru's forehead protector on his arm to keep his hairstyle visible.

Shikamaru's introduction to the series occurs during the Chunin Exams, ninja evaluations held every two years for rank advancement. He belongs to Team 10, which also includes Choji Akimichi and Ino Yamanaka. Despite being remarkably unmotivated and striving for a low-effort existence, Shikamaru possesses exceptional intelligence; his IQ is over 200, as assessed by his instructor, Asuma Sarutobi. Shikamaru's primary skill is the Shadow Imitation Technique, a hallmark of his clan, enabling him to fuse his shadow with an opponent's, thereby immobilizing them and compelling them to mirror his actions. Throughout the series, Shikamaru's shadow manipulation abilities evolve. By Part II, he can simultaneously employ multiple shadow techniques and levitate his shadow to interact with tangible objects, such as impaling enemies with shadow tendrils or using them to hurl weapons.

Shikamaru displays a nonchalant attitude towards the exams. In his fight against Temari from Sunagakure, he outmaneuvers her but concedes the match due to depleted chakra reserves. Nevertheless, he stands out as the sole ninja from his group to achieve Chunin status. This promotion stems from the exam supervisors' admiration for his sharp intellect and strategic thinking during the Temari encounter. Following his promotion, Shikamaru leads a squad tasked with stopping Sasuke Uchiha's defection to Otogakure. While his team successfully overcomes the Otogakure ninja obstructing their path, Sasuke ultimately eludes capture.

In the second part of the series, Shikamaru is tasked with finding two Akatsuki members. His team locates them, but the immortal Akatsuki member, Hidan, kills Asuma Sarutobi despite Shikamaru's efforts. After the funeral, Shikamaru, with the remaining members of Team 10 and Kakashi Hatake, seeks revenge. While others face Hidan's partner, Kakuzu, Shikamaru defeats Hidan and ensures his body is lost forever, avenging Asuma. After the battle, Shikamaru promises to protect Kurenai Yuhi and Asuma's daughter. Later, he is assigned to the Fourth Division with Temari and Gaara, serving as a proxy general under Gaara. In the epilogue, Shikamaru, fulfilling his desire from the final battles, marries Temari, has a son named Shikadai Nara, and becomes the advisor to the Seventh Hokage, Naruto.

Shikamaru's presence extends beyond the core Naruto anime and manga, as he appears in seven of the franchise's films. In the second film, he supports Naruto and Sakura in their fight against Haido, a villain with utopian ideals who seeks global domination using a unique power. A short scene in the fourth film depicts Shikamaru battling numerous stone soldiers. In the fifth film, he joins Kakashi and Sai on a mission to locate the Land of Sky's base, as they plot an invasion of Konoha. The sixth film sees Shikamaru, Sakura, and Sai facing off against a chimera summoned by Hiruko. He also joins the fight against the demon Satori in the eighth film. In the ninth film's alternate reality of the Limited Tsukuyomi, Shikamaru is portrayed as overweight, contrasting sharply with his teammate, who takes on the strategist role. The tenth film features Shikamaru leading a team including Naruto, Sakura, Sai, and Hinata to rescue Hanabi Hyuga, who has been kidnapped by an Otsutsuki. Additionally, he participates in a tournament in the third original video animation. Shikamaru is also a playable character in almost all Naruto video games, such as the Clash of Ninja and Ultimate Ninja series, where he sometimes uses Shadow Imitation Technique variations not found in the anime or manga. His Part II appearance debuted in the video game Naruto Shippūden: Gekitō Ninja Taisen! EX 2.

Takashi Yano's light novel, *Shikamaru Hiden: A Cloud Drifting in Silent Darkness*, features Shikamaru as both protagonist and narrator, with illustrations by Kishimoto. Set two years after the Fourth Ninja War, the story follows Shikamaru's mission as the appointed organizer of the newly established Shinobi Union. He is tasked with capturing a renegade ninja who controls the remote Land of Silence and seeks to create a new world order governed by the populace. The novel also delves into his developing connection with Temari, ultimately showing him grappling with the challenge of naming their child, years after the novel's conclusion.

Shikamaru's popularity within the *Naruto* series is reflected in his consistent high rankings in Weekly Shōnen Jump polls, often placing within the top ten and once achieving fourth place. In the most recent poll from 2011, he secured ninth position, ranking after Sasori and before Hinata. A variety of Shikamaru-themed merchandise has been marketed, including action figures, key chains, and patches representing both his appearances in Part I and Part II. NTT customers also recognized him as their sixteenth favorite male anime character with black hair. CyberConnect2 CEO Hiroshi Matsuyama has also stated Shikamaru is one of his most favorite characters from Naruto.

Shikamaru's character has been the subject of commentary in numerous manga, anime, video game, and related media publications. IGN cited Shikamaru as a favorite character, describing him as "the poster child for any card-carrying member of Generation X" due to his apathy and reluctance to exert himself. Reviewing episode 110, IGN lauded Shikamaru's ability to overcome his laziness and assume leadership of the Sasuke Uchiha retrieval team, concurring with his promotion to Chunin. Anime News Network echoed this sentiment, highlighting Shikamaru's emergence as "an unlikely hero" as a key moment in the arc. Meridian, Mississippi, the state's sixth-largest city, serves as the county seat of Lauderdale County and the central hub of the Meridian, Mississippi Micropolitan Statistical Area. Situated along key transportation routes, the city is located 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, Mississippi, 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama, 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana, and 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee.

Founded in 1860 where the Mobile and Ohio Railroad met the Southern Railway of Mississippi, Meridian flourished as a key trading hub, its economy fueled by the railroads and the commodities they carried. A significant portion of the city was destroyed by General William Tecumseh Sherman during the Battle of Meridian in February 1864, during the American Civil War.

Following its post-war reconstruction, the city experienced a "Golden Age," flourishing as Mississippi's largest city from 1890 to 1930 and a prominent Southern manufacturing hub, facilitated by 44 daily train arrivals and departures. Union Station, constructed in 1906, now functions as a comprehensive transportation hub, offering connections to the Meridian Transit System, Greyhound Buses, and Trailways, serving an average of 242,360 passengers annually. Despite an economic slowdown linked to the railroad industry's decline, the city has broadened its economic base, with healthcare, the military, and manufacturing being the leading employers in 2010. While the 2008 census estimated the city's population at 38,232, the surrounding areas, with 232,900 residents within a 45-mile radius (72 km) and 526,500 within a 65-mile radius (105 km), contribute significantly to the city's economy, with labor forces of 104,600 and 234,200 respectively.

The region's economy benefits from Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, two military installations that collectively provide more than 4,000 jobs. NAS Meridian hosts the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy and the state's inaugural Department of Homeland Security office. Key Field, named in honor of Fred and Al Key, who achieved a world endurance flight record in 1935, now accommodates the Air National Guard's 186th Air Refueling Wing and a support center for the Army National Guard's 185th Aviation Brigade. The largest non-military employer in the area is Rush Foundation Hospital, with a workforce of 2,610 individuals.

Meridian boasts a vibrant arts scene and rich history, evidenced by institutions like the Riley Center, the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. Notably, the city once housed two Carnegie libraries, segregated by race. The Carnegie Branch Library, catering to African Americans, was part of a network of such libraries established for Black communities in the segregated South, but it has since been torn down.

The city has been chosen to host the future Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center ( <unk> ). Meridian is the birthplace of Jimmie Rodgers, recognized as the "Father of Country Music." Highland Park features a museum showcasing artifacts from his life and career, along with railroad artifacts from the steam engine period. The park also contains the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, a designated National Historic Landmark and the only existing two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie carousel in the world. Other prominent individuals born in Meridian include Susan Akin, Miss America 1986; James Chaney, an activist murdered in the 1964 Mississippi civil rights workers killings; and Hartley Peavey, the founder of Peavey Electronics, which is based in Meridian. The federal courthouse was where the 1966-1967 trial of suspects in the Chaney murder and two other activists took place; it marked the first instance of a white jury convicting a white official for a civil rights-related homicide.

The land that is now Meridian was once home to the Choctaw Native Americans. In 1830, as part of the Indian Removal, the United States acquired this territory through the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek. Following the treaty's approval, European-American settlers started migrating to the region.

Richard McLemore, Meridian's initial settler, enticed people to the area by giving away land from a federal grant of roughly 2,000 acres (810 ha) to spur regional growth. In 1853, Lewis A. Ragsdale, an Alabama lawyer, acquired the majority of McLemore's property, while John T. Ball, a Kemper County merchant, purchased the remaining 80 acres (0.32 km2). Ragsdale and Ball, now considered the city's founders, then started dividing their land into lots for future construction.

The naming of the settlement was a point of contention among its residents. While Ball and the city's industrial population favored "Meridian," seeing it as a synonym for "junction," the agrarian residents preferred "<unk>," a Native American term for "mad river" derived from a local creek's name. Ragsdale even suggested "Ragsdale City." Ball attempted to appease both sides by alternating "Meridian" and "<unk>" daily on the station house he built for the Mobile and Ohio Railroad. Ultimately, the growing railroad industry brought an influx of workers who favored "Meridian," leading to its permanent placement on the station sign. The town was officially incorporated as Meridian on February 10, 1860.

At the onset of the Civil War in 1861, Meridian was a modest village. Its location as a key railroad intersection prompted the Confederacy to build military facilities there to aid their war efforts. In 1864, during the Battle of Meridian, General William Tecumseh Sherman's troops invaded the city, obliterating the railroads in all directions, along with an arsenal and vast warehouses. His troops also razed a significant portion of the buildings. Sherman allegedly commented that Meridian, including its depots, warehouses, arsenal, hospitals, offices, hotels, and cantonments, was effectively gone. Despite this devastation, the city's railroad lines were quickly restored, resuming operations just 26 working days after the battle. The Reconstruction period saw continued racial tensions, culminating in the 1871 riot that followed a fire damaging numerous businesses.

Following the Civil War, the town flourished, enjoying its "Golden Age" between 1880 and 1910. The expansion of railroads facilitated transportation and attracted new industries, leading to rapid population growth. This surge in population spurred increased commercial activity in the city center. From 1890 to 1930, Meridian held the title of Mississippi's largest city and a prominent manufacturing hub in the South. Many of the city's landmark structures, such as the Grand Opera House (1890), Wechsler School (1894), two Carnegie libraries (1913), and the city's tallest skyscraper, the <unk> Building (1929), were constructed during or shortly after this period.

Fueled by the commission government's success in attracting 90 new industrial plants in 1913 and the burgeoning automobile industry of the 1920s, the city experienced sustained growth. Remarkably, this expansion persisted even through the Stock Market Crash of 1929 and the subsequent Great Depression, with the city continuing to draw new businesses. Reflecting the era's penchant for escapism, the S. H. Kress & Co. building, designed to offer "luxury to the common man," and the Temple Theater, which functioned as a movie house, both opened in downtown Meridian during the height of the Depression. Further bolstering the city, the federal courthouse was constructed in 1933 as a project of the Works Progress Administration (WPA).

The nation's economy, briefly sluggish after the Depression, rebounded with the onset of World War II, revitalizing the railroad industry. Railroads, critical for moving gasoline and scrap metal needed for military vehicle production, once again positioned Meridian as the region's central rail hub. This period of economic growth lasted until the 1950s, when automobiles and the expanding Interstate Highway System overshadowed passenger rail travel. The subsequent downturn in the railroad sector led to substantial job losses and a corresponding decrease in population as workers sought employment elsewhere.

Meridian, Mississippi, played a significant role in the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s, housing a Council of Federated Organizations (COFO) office and other activist groups. James Chaney, alongside local residents and northern volunteers Michael Schwerner, his wife Rita, and Andrew Goodman, collaborated to establish a community center, providing educational programs to empower African Americans to exercise their voting rights. This activism was met with hostility from local whites, leading to frequent violent outbreaks fueled by racial tension. In June 1964, Chaney, Schwerner, and Goodman traveled to Neshoba County to investigate the bombing and burning of a black church. On their return to Meridian that night, they vanished. A large-scale FBI investigation ensued, and two months later, their bodies were discovered buried in an earthen dam.

In the Mississippi civil rights workers murders trial, a federal court in Meridian convicted seven Klansmen, one of whom was a deputy sheriff, for "depriving the victims of their civil rights," while acquitting three others. This marked the first instance of a white jury convicting "a white official in a civil rights killing." The state reopened the case in 2005, bringing charges for the first time, and Edgar Ray Killen was found guilty of manslaughter, receiving a 60-year sentence. Subsequently, Meridian recognized Chaney's legacy by renaming a section of 49th Avenue in his honor and establishing an annual memorial service.

As highways were built in the 1960s, simplifying commutes, people started leaving the city center and relocating to newly developed residential areas to the north. Subsequently, as commercial establishments began relocating from downtown, the city responded by designating several areas as historic districts during the 1970s and 80s. This was done to protect the city's unique architectural style. To further these efforts, the Meridian Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission was established in 1979, followed by the creation of the Meridian Main Street program in 1985.

Meridian Main Street spearheaded multiple initiatives to revitalize the city center, notably building a new Amtrak station in 1997. This station's design was inspired by the original, now-demolished train station from Meridian's prosperous era. Additional projects encompassed the refurbishment of the Rosenbaum Building in 2001 and Weidmann's Restaurant in 2002, alongside advocating for cohesive urban planning. Furthermore, Meridian Main Street, in collaboration with The Riley Foundation, played a key role in the 2006 restoration and adaptation of the historic Grand Opera House, transforming it into the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and the Performing Arts."

Following the transfer of Meridian Main Street's ownership to the Alliance for Downtown Meridian in late 2007, a collaborative revitalization initiative was launched by the Alliance, Meridian Main Street, and the Meridian Downtown Association. The Alliance acts as a central support system, providing staff and resources to the other two organizations while also facilitating communication between them. Although there were plans to renovate the <unk> Building, these were halted by Mayor Cheri Barry in early 2010. Currently, the Alliance is dedicated to fostering downtown development and restoration, with a particular focus on supporting businesses like specialty shops, restaurants, and bars to enhance downtown activity both during the day and at night. The Meridian Downtown Association concentrates on boosting pedestrian traffic through special events, while the Meridian Main Street program aims to bolster existing downtown businesses.

Meridian's location as a railroad hub spurred the growth of numerous hotels to accommodate travelers. Even before its "Golden Age," prominent hotels like the Great Southern and the Grand Avenue were established before 1900. The expansion of railroads and the opening of the original Union Station in 1906 led to the construction of more hotels for passengers and railroad employees. The Elmira Hotel appeared in 1905, followed by the Terminal Hotel in 1910. Hotel Meridian was erected in 1907, and the Union Hotel in 1908. The Union Hotel earned a place on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, while both Hotel Meridian and the Grand Avenue Hotel were recognized as contributing properties within the Meridian Urban Center Historic District.

The city's burgeoning economy fueled the construction of ambitious hotels, exemplified by the eleven-story Lamar Hotel, erected in 1927. This landmark, which was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, was later repurposed as a county annex. In 1988, it received further recognition as a Mississippi Landmark.

Constructed in 1931, the E.F. Young Hotel became a vital part of the African-American business district that flourished west of the city center. During segregation, it stood as one of the few establishments in the city where African-American travelers could secure lodging.

Following suburban expansion in the 1960s and 70s, hotels largely relocated from the city center. The Riley Center's restoration in 2006 spurred demand for a new downtown hotel. While redevelopment of the <unk> Building for this purpose was suggested, restoration work was interrupted by a change in city government. In 2013, the <unk> Preservation Society was established to promote public awareness and advocate for the building's renovation through initiatives like first-floor tours and anniversary celebrations.

Meridian boasts nine historically significant districts recognized by the National Register of Historic Places. Among them is the Meridian Downtown Historic District, formed by merging the former Meridian Urban Center Historic District and the Union Station Historic District. These districts showcase a diverse range of architectural styles, predominantly from the late 1800s and early 1900s, such as Queen Anne, Colonial Revival, Italianate, Art Deco, Late Victorian, and Bungalow. Since 1985, Meridian has utilized a "strong mayor" system, where the mayor, elected city-wide every four years, serves as the chief executive officer. This individual oversees the daily functioning of the city government. Complementing this, the city council, comprised of five members elected every four years from the city's five single-member districts (wards), acts as the legislative body, establishing policies and approving the city's yearly budget.

Thomas from Ward 1, Kenneth Dustin Markham from Ward 2, Barbara Henson from Ward 3, Kim Houston from Ward 4, and Randy Hammon from Ward 5. Pam McInnis holds the position of council clerk. Following Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the city formed a Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the only local DHS in Mississippi. This team is responsible for a nine-county region. With $2.5 million in grants from the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency and other groups, the department initiated training programs for law enforcement officers from other Southern states in passenger rail rescue. They also provide civilian courses in basic handgun use, Boy Scout first aid, hunting, and firearms training. The DHS provides assistance during crises, such as Hurricane Ivan in September 2005, when it helped set up and maintain shelters for 700 evacuees. The city now leads one of the task forces within the Mississippi DHS, which comprises three nine-county teams.
