The city's expansion has been shaped by a complex interplay of social and economic forces. From its establishment until 1970, the city's total population grew in every census, although the growth rates fluctuated significantly, ranging from a high of 165% to a low of 0.02%. A population decrease was recorded in the 1970 census, followed by a slight increase by 1980. Subsequently, the population experienced a gradual decline until the beginning of the 21st century, after which it began to rise again. Between 1980 and 2000, the population decreased by over 14%. According to the 2000 census, the city had a population of 39,968 and a population density of 885.9 inhabitants per square mile (342.0/km2). By 2008, it had become the sixth-largest city in the state, and the population continued to increase as of 2010.

Meridian serves as the central city within its metropolitan area, which in 2009 encompassed Clarke, Kemper, and Lauderdale counties, totaling a population of 106,139. The area within a 45-mile (72 km) radius of Meridian holds 232,900 residents, while a 65-mile (105 km) radius contains 526,500 people.

Despite fluctuations in the city's total population, the number and proportion of non-white residents have consistently increased. The sole decrease in this demographic occurred between 1960 and 1970, coinciding with a significant drop in the city's overall population. According to the 2010 Census, the city's racial composition was as follows: 61.55% African American, 35.71% White, 0.9% Asian, 0.2% Native American, less than 0.02% Pacific Islander, 0.59% from other races, and 0.89% from two or more races. Individuals of Hispanic or Latino origin, regardless of race, constituted 1.75% of the population.

The 2000 Census data reveals that within the city limits, there were 17,890 housing units, with 15,966 being occupied, including 10,033 family households. Of the occupied households, 31.1% had children under 18, 36.2% were married couples, 23.3% were female-headed households with no husband present, and 37.2% were non-family households. Individuals comprised 33.2% of all households, and 14.0% had a resident 65 years or older living alone. The average household size was 2.39, while the average family size was 3.06. Notably, the average household size has decreased since 1970, when it was 3.04. Meridian's median age has also increased from 30.4 in 1970 to 34.6 in 2000.

In this city, the median household income was $25,085, while the median family income reached $31,062. Men reported a median income of $29,404, noticeably higher than the $19,702 for women. The city's per capita income was $15,255. Approximately 24.6% of families and 28.6% of the overall population lived below the poverty line, with a significant 40.8% of those under 18 and 22.0% of those 65 and older also experiencing poverty.

Meridian and the surrounding Lauderdale County exhibit a strong religious presence. Approximately 65.2% of the county's residents identify with a religious group, exceeding the national average of 50.2%. In 2000, Southern Baptists constituted the largest segment of affiliated individuals at 30,068 (59.0%), followed by the United Methodist Church with 9,469 members (18.6%), and the Catholic Church with 1,872 adherents (3.7%).

Jewish immigrants from Germany and Eastern Europe significantly contributed to Meridian's economic growth by establishing various businesses and services. Congregation Beth Israel was established in 1868, preceding the city's prosperous "Golden Age." Meridian once boasted Mississippi's largest Jewish population, reaching 575 in 1927. Currently, the Jewish community has dwindled to fewer than 40 residents, predominantly elderly individuals.

Meridian is situated in Lauderdale County, within Mississippi's North Central Hills region. The United States Census Bureau reports the city's total area as 45.9 square miles (119 square kilometers), with 45.1 square miles (117 square kilometers) being land and 0.8 square miles (2.1 square kilometers) being water. Positioned along key highways, Meridian is 93 miles (150 kilometers) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 kilometers) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 kilometers) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; 231 miles (372 kilometers) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee; and 297 miles (478 kilometers) west of Atlanta, Georgia. The landscape around Meridian features cotton and corn fields, interspersed with oak and pine forests, and is characterized by clay hills and the bottom lands of the upper reaches of the <unk> River.

While the city's urban center features altered natural terrain due to grading, the surrounding areas retain a gently undulating landscape. Several small creeks meander throughout the city, and small lakes and wooded areas are located in its northern and southern reaches. A major waterway, <unk> Creek, traverses the southern part of the city, branching into Gallagher's Creek, which bisects the city center. Loper's Creek flows through the far western section, and smaller waterways such as Shearer's Branch, Magnolia Creek, and Robbins Creek are scattered across the city.

Meridian experiences a humid subtropical climate. During the summer months (June to August), the average high temperature hovers around 90°F (32°C), while the average low is approximately 70°F (21°C). In winter (December to February), the average high reaches about 60°F (16°C), and the average low dips to around 35°F (2°C). July is typically the warmest month, with an average high of 92.9°F (33.8°C), while January is the coldest, featuring an average low of 34.7°F (1.5°C).

The city receives an average of 58 to 65 inches (1,490 mm) of precipitation annually, with rainfall distributed relatively evenly throughout the year. March is the wettest month, averaging 6.93 inches (176 mm) of rainfall. Thunderstorms are a frequent source of precipitation, occurring year-round but especially during the summer. Severe thunderstorms, capable of producing damaging winds, large hail, lightning, and heavy rain, occasionally occur, primarily in the spring and secondarily in the fall, also bringing a risk of tornadoes.

In its early days, the local economy heavily relied on railroads. Around the turn of the 20th century, the city was Mississippi's largest, boasting five major rail lines and a daily traffic of 44 trains. The city's economic prosperity was tied not only to the railroads themselves but also to the goods they carried, like timber and cotton. This rail-centered industry made the city a significant economic force in the state and region from approximately 1890 to 1930. Although the economy experienced a slowdown with the decline of railroading in the 1950s, the city has since transitioned from a predominantly rail-based economy to a more diverse one, with healthcare, the military, and manufacturing now serving as the primary employers.

Meridian, Lauderdale County, and Marion benefit from the East Mississippi Business Development Corporation, established in 1996 by local business leaders. Despite the city's civilian labor force being only 15,420 as of April 2010, it acts as a central point for employment, commerce, healthcare, and cultural events due to its location within a 45-mile (72 km) radius of 232,900 people (with a labor force of 104,600) and a 65-mile (105 km) radius of 526,500 people (with a labor force of 234,200). The majority of Lauderdale County's workforce (80%) lives within the county, and 90% reside within a 45-mile radius.

As of April 2010, Lauderdale County's healthcare sector employed 6,260 individuals. Rush Hospital stands out as the largest healthcare employer in the area with 2,610 employees, trailed by East Mississippi State Hospital (1,500 employees) and Anderson Hospital (1,475 employees). Meridian houses three hospitals alongside numerous other healthcare-related establishments. Jeff Anderson Regional Medical Center offers services such as cardiovascular surgery, a Level II newborn intensive care unit, and a dedicated health and fitness center. Rush Foundation Hospital, along with Rush Health Systems, manages the Specialty Hospital of Meridian, providing extended care for patients needing longer hospital recovery periods. Riley Hospital features two centers specializing in stroke treatment and rehabilitation. Additional healthcare resources in Meridian include Alliance Health Center and East Mississippi State Hospital, which has been serving the community since 1882.

Retail plays a significant role in the county's economy, employing 5,280 individuals as of April 2010. The city sees approximately $2 billion in annual retail spending. Bonita Lakes Mall, spanning 633,685 square feet (58,871 m2), houses more than 100 retail options, including department stores, specialty stores, dining establishments, and a United Artists Theatres. The completion of Phase I of Meridian Crossroads, a 375,000-square-foot (34,800 m2) shopping center in the Bonita Lakes area, in November 2007, significantly enhanced the local retail scene. Furthermore, the North Hills Street shopping area has grown, with new retail and office spaces opening near the Highway 19 Walmart Supercenter in March 2007.

Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, two military installations in the area, contribute over 4,000 jobs to local residents. NAS Meridian trains naval carrier pilots and other enlisted personnel and hosts the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy (RCTA), which offers narcotics training to law enforcement agencies in numerous southeastern states. The city also houses the state's first local Department of Homeland Security, making it a leader in a nine-county regional response team and a twenty-nine-county regional response task force. Key Field, the location of Fred and Al Key's record-breaking endurance flight in 1935, now serves as home to the Air National Guard's 186th Air Refueling Wing and a support facility for the Army National Guard's 185th Aviation Brigade. The site also features an aviation history exhibit and Meridian's Aviation Museum.

In April 2010, Lauderdale County's manufacturing sector employed 2,850 individuals. Peavey Electronics Corporation, a manufacturer of guitars, amplifiers, and audio equipment since 1965, is headquartered in the city. Additional companies with operations in the area are Avery Dennison, Structural Steel Services, Sara Lee, Tower Automotive, and <unk> Corporation. Furthermore, the city boasts four industrial parks.

The MSU Riley Center in downtown Meridian generates income through tourism, arts, and entertainment. Each year, the Riley Center draws over 60,000 visitors to the city center for various events, including conferences, meetings, and shows. Loeb's Department Store, a long-standing Mississippi clothing institution located on Front Street, has been owned and operated by four generations of the same family. Since its establishment in 1887 by Alex Loeb, the store has been a purveyor of high-quality men's and women's apparel.

Meridian boasts a rich artistic heritage spanning over a century, supporting numerous arts and cultural organizations and a vibrant calendar of cultural events. The Meridian Art League, one of the city's earliest art institutions, was founded in February 1933. Initially, art exhibitions took place in the Lamar Hotel in downtown Meridian. In 1949, the organization rebranded as the Meridian Art Association and began hosting exhibitions at various venues throughout the city. Following the closure of the Carnegie Library at 25th Ave and 7th St, the Art Association renovated the building to create the Meridian Museum of Art, providing a permanent space for its displays. The museum opened its doors in 1970 and has since presented a diverse array of rotating exhibitions and educational programs for students and adults. Each year, over thirty exhibitions showcase a wide range of artistic expressions, from traditional decorative arts to ethnographic and tribal artifacts, photography, crafts, and various other art forms. The museum's collection also encompasses 18th and 19th-century portraits, 20th-century photography, and a selection of sculptures.

Established in 1978, the Meridian Council for the Arts (MCA) serves as the official arts agency for both Meridian and Lauderdale County. The MCA manages the Community Art Grants program, the yearly <unk> Festival, various workshops, and other unique events. It collaborates with numerous arts organizations in the area, such as the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. The Meridian Little Theatre, a subscription-based community theater dating back to 1932, is one of the oldest in the South, entertaining over 22,000 residents and visitors each season, making it the most attended community theater in Mississippi. The Meridian Symphony Orchestra (<unk>), established in 1961, held its inaugural concert in 1962 and its first full season in 1963. In 1965, the orchestra featured its first international soloist, Elena <unk>. The Orchestra assisted the Meridian Public School District in creating its own orchestra and strings programs and contributed to the development of the Meridian Symphony Chorus. Dr. Claire Fox Hillard, the current conductor, has been with the orchestra since 1991. The <unk> commemorated its 50th anniversary in February 2011 with a performance by Itzhak Perlman.

Constructed in 1889 by half-brothers Israel Marks and Levi Rothenberg, the city's original Grand Opera House was a prominent venue that showcased renowned artists and productions, debuting with a German troupe's performance of Johann Strauss II's "The Gypsy Baron." The opera house ceased operations in the late 1920s due to the Great Depression and remained derelict for almost seven decades. In 2000, a $10 million donation from the Riley Foundation, established locally in 1998, initiated the building's refurbishment, complemented by $15 million from municipal, regional, and national grants. The renovation concluded in September 2006, and the venue reopened as the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and Performing Arts." Featuring a 950-seat auditorium for live shows, a 200-seat studio theater, and 30,000 square feet of conference facilities, the Riley Center draws over 60,000 visitors each year to downtown Meridian for various events, including conferences, meetings, and performances.

Meridian is rightfully celebrated as an architectural gem, boasting one of the most well-preserved collections of turn-of-the-century buildings in the United States. Architecture students from across the country and Canada frequently visit Meridian as part of their studies, drawn by the numerous structures designed by prominent architects. Highland Park is home to the sole residence in the Southern US designed by Louis S. Curtiss, a Canadian-born architect renowned for pioneering the glass curtain wall skyscraper. The Frank Fort-designed <unk> Building is widely regarded as a premier Art Deco skyscraper in the US, often likened to Detroit's famous Fisher Building. Wallace Neff, a distinguished California architect, also left his mark on Meridian, designing several homes there and in the adjacent Alabama Black Belt. Neff had relatives who were railroad executives in Meridian and Selma, and he would accept commissions in the area during slow periods in California. His work is largely concentrated on Poplar Springs Drive, where his <unk> Poplar Springs Drive is frequently compared to Falcon Lair, Rudolph Valentino's Beverly Hills estate. Sadly, one Neff creation was lost to an expansion of Anderson Hospital in 1990, and another in Marion Park was destroyed by fire in the 1950s. The Meridian Post Office, notable for its interior crafted entirely from bronze and Verde marble, stands as a prime example of the type of Post Office structures erected in prosperous cities during the 1920s. Originally featuring <unk> lighting, regrettably removed during a 1960s renovation, these fixtures now reside in private homes on Poplar Springs Drive and in North Hills.

Meridian is slated to be the home of the Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center ( <unk> ), an idea approved by the Mississippi Legislature in 2001. In 2006, the legislature pledged $4 million in funding, contingent on private donors raising $8 million. The city contributed $50,000 to the project in September 2007. The proposed <unk> would occupy 175 acres (71 ha) at Bonita Lakes, featuring an outdoor amphitheater, an indoor concert hall, and a Hall of Fame dedicated to Mississippi artists. The Hall of Fame itself will be situated downtown in the former Montana's building, acquired along with the adjacent Meridian Hotel building in July 2010 for $300,000. To promote the future Hall of Fame, the <unk> unveiled its Walk of Fame outside the Riley Center in February 2009, with the inaugural star honoring Meridian native Jimmie Rodgers. The second star, revealed in September of the same year, recognized Mississippi blues legend B.B. King. The <unk> intends to include many more Mississippi-born celebrities on the Walk of Fame, with potential honorees including Morgan Freeman, Jimmy Buffett, Elvis Presley, and Conway Twitty, among others.

The <unk> Shrine Temple Theater is another prominent venue in the city for large-scale productions. It boasts a 778-pipe Robert Morgan organ, a rare example of a theater organ remaining in its original installation within the state. During the silent film era, the Temple, with its 1800-seat capacity, thrived as it possessed one of the largest stages in the U.S., surpassed only by New York City's Roxy Theater. Currently accommodating 1576 people, the Temple hosts a variety of events throughout the year, including live stage performances, plays, concerts, <unk> Shrine activities, and public showings of classic films.

The Jimmie Rodgers Museum in Highland Park features "The Singing Brakeman's" original guitar, memorabilia from his life and career, and railroad equipment from the steam engine period. The museum grounds include outdoor memorials and a vintage steam locomotive. Meridian, Rodgers' birthplace, holds a Mississippi Blues Trail marker recognizing his pivotal role in shaping Mississippi blues music, making it the first location outside the Delta to receive this honor. Meridian has hosted the State Games of Mississippi, an annual, statewide multi-sport competition inspired by the Olympic Games, since 1992. Meridian Regional Airport, situated at Key Field on Airport Boulevard South, provides air transportation to the city. It is located 3 miles (4.8 km) southwest of the city center. The airport boasts Mississippi's longest public runway, measuring 10,004 feet (3,049 m). Operating since 1930, the airport offers daily flights to Dallas/Fort Worth, TX.

Faced with high maintenance costs during the Great Depression, the city considered closing the airport. However, in 1935, airport managers Fred and Al Key devised a plan to save it. The brothers flew their plane, the "Ole Miss," continuously over the city from June 4 to July 1, 1935. Their 27-day flight, lasting 653 hours and 34 minutes, garnered enough attention and financial support to keep the airport open. Consequently, the airport, named Key Field in their honor, stands as a testament to the Key brothers, whose flight endurance record remains unmatched in conventional aviation.

Meridian's early public education system was established following the 1870 Mississippi Constitution. From 1870 to 1885, the City Council appointed trustees to the Board of School Directors, which oversaw the operation of schools. Prior to 1884, the city's schools were private, serving only about 400 students. Meridian's first publicly owned school was not built until September 1884. The initial public school for African American students was held in rented space at St. Paul Methodist Church. In January 1888, the Mississippi Legislature revised the city charter, enabling Meridian to manage its own municipal school district. Subsequently, in March of the same year, voters approved $30,000 in bonds to fund the construction of new public schools, leading to the construction of Wechsler School in 1894, the first brick public school building in Mississippi built for black students.

Originating from its initial district and subsequent expansions, the Meridian Public School District has expanded to its present configuration, encompassing six elementary schools, three middle schools, and three high schools. The city also hosts a number of private educational institutions, such as Lamar School, Calvary Christian School, Community Christian School, and St. Patrick's Catholic School. Meridian High School, the district's primary high school, is situated on a 37-acre (15 ha) campus, featuring six buildings and 111 classrooms, and serves approximately 1,500 students in grades 10-12.

Meridian boasts two institutions for post-secondary education. Meridian Community College, established in 1937 and situated at 910 Highway 19 N, provides four semesters of free tuition to graduates of Meridian Public and Lauderdale County School Districts, as well as homeschooled students within Lauderdale County. Initially named Meridian Junior College and housed at Meridian High School, the college relocated to its current site in 1965. Following desegregation legislation, it merged with T.J. Harris Junior College, formerly serving African-American students, in 1970. In 1987, the institution's name was changed to Meridian Community College to better represent the breadth of opportunities it offers to the expanding local community. Additionally, Mississippi State University maintains a campus within the city. In the Fall of 2008, the college had an enrollment of 763 students from 33 counties across Mississippi and several counties in Alabama.

The Meridian @-@ Lauderdale County Public Library, situated at the intersection of 7th Street and 26th Avenue, serves the city of Meridian. Originally, the city had two Carnegie libraries, constructed in 1913, one for black residents and another for white residents. The Fortnightly Book and Magazine Club, established by a group of women in the 1880s, initiated fundraising efforts to create a city library. Their collected books formed the initial basis of the library's collection. With widespread community support, the club sought assistance from philanthropist Andrew Carnegie through city leader Israel Marks. The black library was erected at 13th Street and 28th Avenue on land donated by St. Paul Methodist Church, while the white library was housed in a building previously owned by members of the First Presbyterian Church of Meridian, sold to the city on September 25, 1911. Notably, the African American library was the state's only library for blacks until after World War I and the nation's only Carnegie library built for African Americans. These two libraries operated until 1967 when, due to the Civil Rights Act of 1964, they integrated, merged their collections, and relocated to their present site. In 1970, the former white library was renovated to become the Meridian Museum of Art, while the original African American library was torn down on May 28, 2008.

Papa Stour, an island in the Shetland archipelago of Scotland, is home to fewer than twenty residents, some of whom arrived following a 1970s campaign to attract new inhabitants. Situated west of mainland Shetland and spanning 828 hectares (3.2 square miles), it ranks as the eighth largest Shetland island. The island's coastline is sculpted by the sea's erosion of its fragile volcanic rock, resulting in a remarkable array of caves, sea stacks, arches, blowholes, and cliffs. Papa Stour and its adjacent waters support a rich variety of wildlife. The island's western coast is designated as a Site of Special Scientific Interest, while the surrounding marine environment is recognized as a Special Area of Conservation.

This island features multiple Neolithic burial chambers and the ruins of Duke Hakon's 13th-century residence, a relic of the Norse era. Its population peaked at over 380 in the 1800s, coinciding with the establishment of a fishing station at <unk> in West Voe. Afterward, the population dwindled consistently, but it has since rebounded from a nadir of 16 in the 1970s.

Papa Stour sits at the southwestern tip of St Magnus Bay and features a dramatic, uneven coastline stretching for 34 kilometers (21 miles). This coastline is marked by many small inlets and four significant voes (bays). In the south, Leir Voe (from the Old Norse for "harbor bay") offers the best protection for boats, and its neighboring cliffs boast a naturally formed rock arch. To the east, Housa Voe (from the Old Norse for "house bay") is more exposed but serves as the island's primary harbor and the departure point for the ferry.

Holm and Maiden Stack stand as sentinels guarding the harbor's southern entrance. Holm, a tidal island, once served as a leper colony until the 18th century, though some believe many of its inhabitants suffered from vitamin deficiency rather than leprosy. Maiden Stack's name originates from a 14th-century tale. Lord Thorvald is said to have built a small house, whose remnants are still visible, on its summit to shield his daughter from male suitors. However, his plans were thwarted when she left, only to be found pregnant; another version claims she successfully eloped with her fisherman lover. A belt of glacial moraine, approximately 1.5 kilometers long, divides the island's western side. The remaining area largely comprises shallow, stony soil, potentially originating from glacial till. Peat is almost entirely absent, and the volcanic bedrock contributes to the soil's relative fertility. This lack of peat historically resulted in "turf scalping" for fuel, exposing bare rock in the island's interior.

On June 21, 2008, Stuart Hill, the sole inhabitant and proprietor of the 1-hectare (2.5-acre) island of Forvik Holm (which he calls "Forvik Island"), declared its independence, establishing the Crown Dependency of Forvik. Hill asserted that, based on a marriage agreement from 1468 between Norway's King Christian and Scotland's King James III, the island should be regarded as a British crown dependency, separate from both the United Kingdom and the European Union. The UK government did not acknowledge this claim.

The island's geology features diverse volcanic and sedimentary rocks dating back to the Devonian period, when Scotland was part of the Old Red Sandstone Continent, located 10-25 degrees south of the equator. These Old Red Sandstone deposits, formed between 408 and 370 million years ago, originated from the erosion of Silurian rocks uplifted during Pangaea's formation, with the resulting sediment deposited in river deltas. Freshwater Lake Orcadie bordered the eroding mountains, extending from Shetland to the southern Moray Firth. Papa Stour's structure mainly consists of volcanic ash and lava from this era, including bands of solidified rhyolite, alongside a Devonian fish bed at Lamba Banks. Furthermore, the island is scattered with large boulders left behind by Pleistocene glaciation.

The sea's erosion of the island's soft volcanic rock has sculpted a remarkable collection of caves, stacks, arches, blowholes, cliffs, voes, and other formations, considered some of the most impressive in Britain. The 'Holl o' is a cave that cuts entirely through the island's northwest tip, stretching nearly half a mile in length and boasting sufficient width for rowing. 'Hole' (or Christie's) Hole, situated in the southwest, is another striking cave, distinguished by a partial roof collapse in 1981. Papa Stour's waters and surrounding areas are often visited by otters, grey seals, killer whales, and harbour porpoises. The island provides a breeding ground for a diverse array of birds, including Atlantic puffins, Arctic and common terns, and various other species such as Arctic skua, northern fulmar, common guillemot, razorbill, curlew, wheatear, ringed plover, and great black-backed gull. Furthermore, many migratory bird species have been observed on the island.

The island boasts a rich variety of wildflowers, such as mountain everlasting, spring squill, and an unidentified species, alongside the common heather. The western part of the island holds the designation of a Site of Special Scientific Interest, while the surrounding waters are recognized as a Special Area of Conservation. Furthermore, the iconic Shetland Pony is still actively bred on the island.

The island's history of human habitation stretches back to around 3000 BC, evidenced by the remnants of Neolithic burial structures called "heel-shaped cairns." While information about the pre-Celtic and Celtic periods is scarce, the arrival of the Norsemen likely revealed a religious community. The island's name originates from <unk> <unk>, signifying "Big island of the Papar" (Celtic monks), differentiating it from Papa Little, located approximately 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) to the west.

Papa Stour is featured in a 1299 Old Norse manuscript, Shetland's oldest surviving document, which recounts a dramatic event in the household of Duke Hakon Magnusson, the future King Hakon V of Norway. Close to <unk> Voe beach, a stone circle marks the site of a 'ting,' or local assembly. This is where Lord Thorvald <unk> fought and won a duel. He was accused of corruption in the 1299 document and later known as ‘dominus de <unk>’. (His daughter's tragic story is mentioned earlier.) The remnants of Duke Hakon's 13th-century residence can still be seen near <unk> Voe.

Although Shetland officially fell under Scottish rule in 1469, Norwegian landowners retained their estates on Papa Stour until the 17th century. During the 1500s, merchants from Bremen and Hamburg established seasonal trading posts to purchase fish from local fishermen. By the 18th century, the island was owned by two Scottish landowners, Thomas Gifford of Busta and Arthur Nicolson of Lerwick. They oversaw a thriving haaf (Old Norse for "deep sea") fishing industry, conducted during the summer using sixareens, which were six-oared boats.

Established in 1806, the island church commands a view of Kirk Sand in Fore Wick bay. Approximately 300 meters away, situated on the headland between Kirk Sand's western edge and an adjacent bay, possibly lies the location of a more ancient chapel. Locally known as the "blank kirk" and identified by the Ordnance Survey as "the site of a blank chapel dating back to around the twelfth century," legend suggests supernatural forces disrupted its construction. It's said that each day's progress was undone nightly, until the cornerstones were miraculously relocated to the church's current location, where construction proceeded without incident. Archaeological digs in 2004 unearthed mostly sizable rhyolite blocks and a fragment of whalebone rib, hinting at the potential validity of the local lore.

During the 1800s, a fishing station began operating in West Voe, and Papa Stour's population grew to at least 360 residents. However, fuel became scarce, and steam drifters caused a drop in fishing, leading to a population decline starting in the 1870s. Around this time, another unusual event occurred: Edwin Lindsay, an Indian army officer and the 6th Earl of Balcarres' son, was deemed insane after refusing to participate in a duel. As a result, he was sent to Papa Stour in disgrace and held prisoner for 26 years until Catherine Watson, a Quaker preacher, secured his release in 1835. Lindsay's Well, a spring in the southern part of the island, marks the location where he was permitted to bathe.

Horizontal water mills, also called Norse or Clack Mills, are well-represented near Dutch Loch. These mills were typically two-story structures with turf roofs, constructed into hillsides to provide access to the upper level where the millstone was located. The interior housed a stationary lower millstone and a rotating upper millstone, powered by water cascading onto paddles underneath. Some of these mills remained operational on Papa Stour until the early 1900s, and a functioning example can still be found on the Burn of [location], at [location] in southern Mainland Shetland.

Like many small Scottish islands, Papa Stour's population reached its highest point in the 1800s, followed by a substantial decrease (similar to Mingulay). The island's school shut down by 1970, and the population dwindled to sixteen mostly elderly inhabitants. However, an advertisement in Exchange and Mart, offering a free croft and five sheep to newcomers, successfully countered this decline, attracting numerous applications. The 1981 census reported a population of 33. Unfortunately, by 2005, serious disputes among islanders, resulting in legal proceedings, caused the population to drop to 20, leading to departures and the school's closure. By early 2008, the population plummeted to just nine after a family of seven relocated. The 2011 census recorded a usual resident population of 15, while overall Scottish island populations increased by 4% to 103,702 during the decade from 2001 to 2011.

On the evening of March 28, 1930, the Aberdeen trawler Ben Doran ran aground on the Ve Skerries, located 3 miles northwest of Papa Stour, while en route to Scalloway to unload its catch. Although the weather was initially favorable, the wreck wasn't discovered until the next day by a passing trawler. By the time the coastguard and local volunteers mobilized rescue efforts (as Shetland had no lifeboat station then), the weather had worsened, making it impossible to reach the skerries. A request for the Stromness lifeboat from Orkney, just 120 miles distant, was made, but it was too late to be effective. Tragically, all nine crew members died in the shipwreck. Only three bodies were recovered: James Mitchell, who was returned to Aberdeen, and J. Cormack and J.R. <unk>, who were buried in Scalloway.

In February 1940, the SS Highcliffe cargo ship was shipwrecked on <unk> Holm due to dense fog. Fortunately, the weather was mild, and the only losses were the vessel and its goods. Later, in 1967, the Aberdeen trawler Juniper was grounded in Lyra Sound, at the base of towering 60-meter (200-foot) cliffs. The <unk> lifeboat successfully saved all 12 crew members, and the coxswain was honored with the RNLI silver medal for his bravery during the rescue.

The most recent shipwreck near Papa Stour happened on December 9, 1977, when the Aberdeen-based trawler Elinor Viking, captained by Alec Flett, ran aground on the Ve Skerries. Although the local lifeboat responded, severe weather prevented it from approaching the stricken vessel. Alec Webster, the Coastguard Station Officer in Lerwick, then requested assistance from a volunteer crew operating a British Airways Sikorsky helicopter from Sumburgh Airport. In spite of the gale-force winds, the helicopter crew successfully winched all the trawler's crew to safety within hours of the grounding. Their bravery was subsequently recognized with several awards. This incident, which resulted in no fatalities, led to the construction of a lighthouse on the skerries in 1979 and may have also spurred the establishment of the current Search and Rescue helicopter unit at Sumburgh Airport.

Crofting remains central to the island's way of life. While sheep farming is the primary agricultural activity, a variety of livestock such as cattle, pigs, goats, chickens, ducks, and geese are also raised. A post office is located at the pier, but there are no shops. Mains electricity was only introduced to the island in the late 1900s. The journey lasts 45 minutes, and despite the unk's ability to transport vehicles, there is only a single short road on the unk. Visiting yachts can find good shelter in the four main voes, but the strong currents in both the Sound of Papa and the northwest require caution.

"Angel of Death" begins Reign in Blood, the 1986 album by American thrash metal band Slayer. Guitarist Jeff Hanneman penned the song's lyrics and music, drawing inspiration from Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who performed human experiments at the Auschwitz concentration camp during World War II. The song's content resulted in persistent accusations of Nazi sympathies and racism directed at Slayer.

Despite the controversy it generated and its role in delaying the release of Reign in Blood , "Angel of Death" has become a staple of Slayer's live performances, appearing on all their live albums and DVDs, and has also been included in various films. Critics have praised the song, with AllMusic's Steve Huey calling it a "classic."

While touring with Slayer, guitarist Jeff Hanneman became fascinated by Josef Mengele, the Nazi physician, after reading books about him. This interest directly inspired the lyrics for "Angel of Death." Hanneman recalled being struck by the disturbing nature of Mengele's actions and how those impressions lingered, ultimately shaping the song's themes when the band began working on the album.

The song's lyrics describe the surgical experiments Josef Mengele performed on inmates at the Auschwitz concentration camp during World War II. Mengele's research involved various groups, including dwarfs and twins, and encompassed both physical and psychological evaluations. "Angel of Death" references specific experiments he carried out, such as surgeries without anesthesia, blood transfusions between twins, endurance tests in isolation, gassing, injections of deadly pathogens, sex change operations, organ and limb removal, and other unspecified procedures.

The lyric "together, joining heads... 'til you rip yourselves apart," alludes to the accusation that Josef Mengele surgically conjoined twins, resulting in one being deformed. This claim, that "the hunchback was sewn to the other child, back to back, their wrists back to back too," originated with Auschwitz survivor Vera Alexander during the 1961 trial of Adolf Eichmann, the "architect of the Holocaust." Alexander testified that Mengele "sewed the veins together," transforming the twins "into Siamese twins." The allegation gained broader recognition after Alexander appeared in the 1985 documentary *The Search for Mengele*, a source cited by numerous authors, including Mengele expert Gerald Posner.

The controversial lyrics in "Angel of Death" were a factor in delaying the release of Slayer's 1986 album, Reign in Blood. Def Jam Records, Slayer's label, faced resistance from their distributor, Columbia Records, who declined to release the album, citing concerns about the lyrical themes and deeming the artwork "too graphic." Ultimately, Geffen Records distributed Reign in Blood on October 7, 1986. However, due to the controversy surrounding the album, it was not included in Geffen Records' official release schedule.
